positions.stakeholder_concern: For sensor-based devices, model-level benchmarking alone may not capture performance, because the final clinical or measurement output also depends on the sensor interface, signal acquisition, signal processing, software, and interactions among these components.
positions.requested_fda_action: Where relevant, complement model-level competency assessment with system-level verification of the entire device pathway rather than relying on model benchmarking alone.
positions.public_summary: Accepts competency-based benchmarking but notes it may be insufficient alone for sensor-based devices, where outputs depend on sensor interface, signal acquisition, processing, software, and their interactions. Asks FDA to pair model-level assessment with system-level verification of the full device pathway.
positions.source_passage: Model-level benchmarking is important, but for a sensor-based medical device it may not be sufficient by itself. The final clinical or measurement output can also depend on the sensor interface, signal acquisition, signal processing, software, and interactions among these components. ... Therefore, where relevant, model-level competency assessment should be complemented by system-level verification of the device pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter emphasizes that controlled physiological signal inputs give known, repeatable test conditions that allow verification of device response and re-testing of the same condition after a design change, but only cover the portion of performance assessable under controlled conditions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize controlled-input testing as a valid method for verifying the bench-testable portion of device performance and for re-evaluation following design changes, while relying on appropriate clinical evidence for real-world performance.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports using controlled, repeatable physiological signal inputs to verify device response and to re-test after design changes, while noting such testing covers only the portion of performance assessable under controlled conditions; real-world performance should be established through appropriate clinical evidence.
positions.source_passage: Controlled physiological signals are useful because they provide known and repeatable inputs. Manufacturers can verify how the device responds to a defined condition and repeat the same condition after a design change. Their role is to verify the portion of device performance that can reasonably be evaluated under controlled input conditions, while real-world clinical performance is addressed through appropriate clinical evidence.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter emphasizes that real patient data and controlled simulation serve distinct verification purposes and are not interchangeable: real data captures clinically observed physiological variability and representativeness, while simulation provides repeatable, controlled coverage for robustness, boundary, stress, and regression testing.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage does not state an explicit request; it implicitly suggests FDA treat simulated/synthetic inputs and real patient data as answering different evaluation questions rather than as substitutes.
positions.public_summary: The commenter distinguishes the roles of real patient data and controlled simulation in evaluation: real data establishes clinical representativeness and physiological variability, while simulation enables repeatable, controlled robustness, boundary, stress, and regression testing. No explicit agreement or disagreement with FDA's approach is stated.
positions.source_passage:
Real patient data and simulation answer different verification questions. Real patient data is important for representing clinically observed physiological variability. Controlled simulation is useful for creating known and repeatable conditions for robustness, boundary, stress and regression testing.
Real patient data supports clinical representativeness. Controlled simulation supports repeatability and controlled coverage of defined test conditions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Simulated or played-back physiological signals reproduce only the parameters the simulation method was designed and characterized to reproduce; physical factors such as tissue characteristics, optical path, sensor geometry and device-to-body coupling remain outside the scope of a recorded-waveform playback, so simulation-based evidence can overstate real-world coverage.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require that the boundary of any simulation be made explicit, with the represented parameters and conditions, the test purpose, and the stated limitations documented when simulated inputs are used as evidence.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts simulated physiological inputs as evidence but asks FDA to require explicit boundaries: a simulation represents only parameters it was designed and characterized to reproduce, excluding factors like tissue characteristics, sensor geometry, and device-to-body coupling; its test purpose and limitations should be stated.
positions.source_passage:
The boundary should be explicit. A simulator represents a defined subset of physiological and physical conditions. For example, in optical physiological sensing, performance may be affected by tissue characteristics, optical path, sensor geometry, device-to-body coupling and other physical interactions. Playing back a clinically recorded waveform represents the waveform, while those additional physical factors remain outside the scope of that playback.
A simulated physiological signal therefore represents only the parameters and conditions that the simulation method has been designed and characterized to reproduce. Its test purpose and limitations should be stated.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Simulated or synthetic inputs have a bounded role limited to situations requiring controlled, repeatable, edge-case, or post-modification regression testing, and cannot substitute for clinical evidence where real-world anatomy, physiology, or use conditions materially affect performance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize simulation as appropriate for controlled input testing, repeatability, edge/stress conditions, and retesting after modifications, while requiring clinical confirmation whenever human anatomy, physiology, use conditions, or other real-world factors materially affect device performance.
positions.public_summary: The commenter accepts a role for simulation, specifying it is best suited to controlled, repeatable, edge-case, and post-modification testing, but states clinical confirmation remains necessary where human anatomy, physiology, use conditions, or other real-world factors materially affect device performance.
positions.source_passage: Simulation is most useful when a manufacturer needs to control a specific input, repeat the same test consistently, explore defined edge or stress conditions, or reproduce the same test after a modification. Clinical confirmation remains necessary when human anatomy, physiology, use conditions or other real-world factors materially affect device performance.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that benchmark validity may be judged by dataset size rather than by whether the test answers a defined verification question with known provenance, ground truth, and limitations. A smaller, well-characterized dataset may provide stronger evidence than a large dataset of unclear origin.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should frame benchmarks around an explicit verification question (what is tested, input provenance, reference/ground truth, expected result, method limits, reproducibility) and emphasize fitness for purpose, traceability, reproducibility, and clearly stated limitations when assessing benchmark validity.
positions.public_summary: Supports benchmarking but urges FDA to anchor benchmark validity in a defined verification question rather than dataset scale, emphasizing fitness for purpose, data provenance, ground truth, reproducibility, and stated method limitations; notes smaller well-characterized datasets can offer stronger evidence.
positions.source_passage:
The purpose of verification is to provide credible evidence for a defined requirement or risk. A medical-device benchmark should therefore start with a clear verification question.
What is being tested? What does the input represent? Where did it come from? What is the reference or ground truth? What result is expected? What are the limits of the test method? Can the test be reproduced?
A smaller, well-characterized dataset may provide stronger evidence for a specific verification purpose than a much larger dataset with unclear provenance, ground truth, intended use or limitations. We encourage FDA to emphasize fitness for purpose, traceability, reproducibility and clearly stated limitations when considering benchmark validity.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without pre-planned, reusable verification tests, changes to software, firmware, algorithms or AI models cannot be reliably compared against an established premarket baseline.
positions.requested_fda_action: Encourage that premarket verification be designed, where practical, for later reuse as a regression baseline documenting device version, test data version, test condition, expected result, acceptance criteria and actual result, with affected tests repeated under the same controlled conditions after a change.
positions.public_summary: Supports using premarket testing as a re-evaluation baseline, but asks that verification be designed for reuse as a regression baseline with specified elements (device and test data versions, conditions, expected results, acceptance criteria, actual results), repeated under identical conditions after changes.
positions.source_passage:
Where practical, premarket verification should be designed so that relevant tests can later be reused as a regression baseline. A baseline may identify:
Device version + Test data version + Test condition + Expected result + Acceptance criteria + Actual result
After a relevant software, firmware, algorithm, AI model or other device change, the affected tests can be repeated under the same controlled conditions and compared with the established baseline.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that re-testing obligations after post-deployment modifications be proportionate to the nature and potential impact of the change rather than uniform.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should keep the scope of re-testing risk-based, allowing targeted regression testing for limited modifications while requiring broader re-verification for changes affecting sensing, signal processing, algorithm behavior, or clinical output.
positions.public_summary: The commenter supports scaling post-modification re-testing to risk: limited changes would warrant targeted regression testing, while changes affecting sensing, signal processing, algorithm behavior, or clinical output would warrant broader re-verification.
positions.source_passage: The scope of re-testing should remain risk-based: a limited modification may require targeted regression testing, while a change that may affect sensing, signal processing, algorithm behavior or clinical output may require broader re-verification.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned with reliably detecting whether a device's behavior has changed following a modification, noting that repeatability is a principal strength of simulation when the same controlled challenge is applied before and after the change.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize repeatable simulation-based testing as a means of comparing device behavior before and after modifications, while relying on clinical and real-world evidence to address performance beyond the defined scope of the simulated test.
positions.public_summary: The commenter describes repeatable simulation as a way to detect whether known device behavior has changed after a modification, applying the same controlled challenge before and after, with clinical and real-world evidence covering performance outside the simulation's defined scope.
positions.source_passage: Repeatability is one of simulation's main strengths in this context. Its purpose is to determine whether a known aspect of device behavior has changed when the same controlled challenge is applied before and after a modification. Clinical and real-world evidence continue to address performance beyond the defined scope of the simulated test.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter holds that although generative AI may call for new verification methods, the established regulatory logic still applies: evidence should be proportionate to intended use and risk, test methods should be used only within their demonstrated scope, and changes potentially affecting safety or effectiveness should be re-evaluated.
positions.requested_fda_action: Maintain the existing risk- and intended-use-based evidentiary logic when evaluating GenAI-enabled devices, while accommodating new verification methods and ensuring each method is applied within its validated scope and that safety-relevant changes trigger re-evaluation.
positions.public_summary: The commenter supports retaining familiar regulatory logic for generative AI devices—evidence matched to intended use and risk, test methods applied only within their demonstrated scope, and re-evaluation of changes affecting safety or effectiveness—while acknowledging that new verification methods may be needed.
positions.source_passage: We believe GenAI may require new verification methods, while the underlying regulatory logic remains familiar: evidence should be appropriate to intended use and risk, each test method should be applied within its demonstrated scope, and changes that may affect safety or effectiveness should be re-evaluated.
